content: Patients with severe influenza, whether caused by novel influenza A viruses or other strains, may require mechanical ventilation (invasive or non-invasive) and/or vasopressor therapy. Even if they do not meet the standard criteria for severe disease, individuals with novel influenza A associated with high mortality or unknown risk of severe disease should still be classified as having severe influenza. Risk factors for severe influenza were identified through a systematic review of observational studies. The median age of patients in these studies was 57 years, and the risk of severe disease increased significantly with age, particularly for those aged 65 years or older. Major risk factors for developing severe disease include immunocompromising conditions, cardiovascular disease, neurological disease, and chronic respiratory disease. Additional risk factors include malignancy, pregnancy, and diabetes. Patients aged 85 years or older, or those of any age with multiple major risk factors, are at extremely high risk of hospitalization. Patients infected with zoonotic influenza viruses, such as HPAI A(H5N1), HPAI A(H5N6), and HPAI/LPAI A(H7N9), are also considered high-risk due to their association with high mortality in humans. To support clinical guidelines, a systematic review of observational studies was conducted to identify risk factors for severe disease in patients with non-severe influenza. This review focused on fully adjusted results and primarily used odds ratios (ORs) as the measure of association. Age was strongly associated with increased odds of hospitalization, with the risk rising significantly for every 20 years of age. Other factors associated with increased odds of hospitalization include HIV, immunodeficiency, malignancy, pregnancy, renal disease, and chronic respiratory diseases. Conditions such as anemia, asthma, hypertension, and liver disease were found to have little or no association with increased hospitalization risk. Regarding mortality, age and the Charlson comorbidity index were strongly associated with increased odds of all-cause mortality in non-severe patients. Smoking was also linked to higher mortality risk. However, conditions like cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and hypertension showed little or no association with increased mortality. Antiviral drugs for influenza target specific stages of the viral life cycle, including the M2 ion channel, fusion, RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp), and neuraminidase. Drugs targeting RdRp are further classified into nucleoside RNA polymerase inhibitors and cap-snatching inhibitors. Resistance to M2 ion channel inhibitors, such as amantadine and rimantadine, is widespread, and these drugs are no longer recommended. Baloxavir marboxil, a cap-snatching inhibitor, is administered as a single oral dose and inhibits the endonuclease activity of the RdRp complex, thereby blocking viral replication. However, resistance mutations have been observed, particularly in children and certain influenza subtypes. Baloxavir is not recommended for use in pregnant or postpartum women due to insufficient safety and efficacy data. It is also excreted in breast milk, and its use during lactation requires caution.
